input.question: How is it possible that everything falls at the same speed regardless of mass? Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct?
input.ground_truth: > Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct? Yes. The "limit of the approximation" is that the mass of the thing dropped is negligible compared to the mass of the Earth. Consider two masses M1 and M2 at a distance R. The gravitational force F between them will be G\*M1\*M2/R^2 , so the acceleration of the first object will be F/M1 = G\*M2/R^2 and the acceleration of the second object will be F/M2 = G\*M1/R^2 The two objects will thus accelerate towards each other at a rate of G\*(M1 + M2)/R^2 . In the case of a feather or hammer on the Earth, M1 is so much larger than M2 that the effects of M2 can be ignored. In this case, both hammer and feather would have the same acceleration.

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a feather and a big rock. If you drop them at the same time on Earth, they both hit the ground at the same time (if there’s no air, like on the Moon). This happens because the Earth pulls everything equally, but a heavy thing needs a little more “push” to move the same way as a light thing. But in the air on Earth, the wind can make the feather fall slower because it’s light and the air pushes back a lot.

But if there’s no air (like on the Moon), both fall at the same speed! This is because of gravity, which is like an invisible rope that pulls everything down at the same rate if we ignore air.

However, this is only *almost* true. If things go very, very fast or are very, very heavy, or if we are not on Earth but near a very big planet, the rules change a little bit. But for most things we drop every day, they fall at the same speed! 🌍🪨🪶
